Title: Judging the accidentally showing of a card

Messages.Author: x5m...@gmx.de
Messages.Body:
There was a discussion about a game at the EC at the conclave. I DONT
want to discuss that game again, but i am interested on some comments
about one aspect. So here is the abstract case.

If the accidentally showing of a card gives the player a big advantage
in the game or is a big disadvantage for another player in the game,
can the "Correction of game state" include the discarding/reshuffling
of the shown card. Thereby not correcting the game state of the cards
in hand/on table, but the state, that the other players did not know
about the card.

Example: The showing of a Delaying tactics causes diffrenet terms on a
Parity Shift. So the player who shows the card does not get 5 point
damage, but gets 5 pool and another player loses the 5 pool. (I am
assuming that it is a big difference if players bluff by saying, they
have a DT, like my players always do, or that you really know, if
somenone has a DT.)

Frank

Following are the tournament rules:

114. Procedural Error - Misrepresentation
Definition: A player is considered to have committed this infraction
when he or she unintentionally misplayed a card or a game rule.

Philosophy: This penalty assumes an unintentional action on behalf of
the player. If the judge believes the misrepresentation was
intentional, see section 160 - Cheating.

Penalty: Caution.

200. Correction of Game State
It is important that the player committing the infraction receive no
benefit in the game for doing so. If no significant game actions have
taken place, play should be backed-up to the point of the error. The
error should then be corrected and the game should proceed forward from
that point. If significant game actions have taken place (such as
moving to the next player's turn or knowledge of another player's
cards), the judge may choose to leave the game undisturbed or may
adjust the game state in some other way (for instance, altering pool or
blood levels) since players have made play decisions based on the
subsequent state of the game.

play group.

Is there, in fact, a rule that states that a methuselah is not
permitted to reveal the contents of their hand to other players?

i.e. Is it actually contary to any _specific_ rule to simply play with
your hand revealed at all times? If so, which one? and is this a Game
Rule (i.e. to be found in the rulebook in a starter) or a Tournement
Rule? (i.e. may or may not apply to casual play, depending on the
tastes of that play group)

frequently out of synch with the supposed actual rules of this game.
(KMW rulebook, btw)

This came up in our group in the case of a defelection being (actually
accidentally) dropped from a players hand, changing the predator's
bleeding decisions. The discussion was, would it be within the rules to
simply hold up your deflection for your predator to see at the
beginning of the turn. (you tend to get the benefit of no big bleed
until its gone or much later in the flow of the game, which can delay
bleed pressure considerably)

It'd be nice to actually have an answer for this question, when next it
is asked.

situation in the other direction because the acting player can be sure
that the player how showed the DT has no DT (or at least one less) in

the change of terms in result to the showing of the card.

>> the (legal) threat of having a DT.
>
> Really? Two players want to influence my decision of the terms of a
> vote. Both players tell me they have a DT. The one showing the DT will
> have a big advantage in the dealing of the terms.

That may be a slight advantage but it's not an important enough advantage
to go throwing away a useful card drawn at a time it's useful, which is
a significant penalty.

Part of the problem here (and I know this because I've seen his
statements about this on the Prince's Conclave and in private E-mail)
is that you insist on looking at forcing a player to discard a card
and redraw as some sort of a "neutral" thing. In truth, forcing
a discard of a card a player has been fortunate enough to draw at a
critical moment which is useful is not a neutral thing! He has
paid for the possession of that card by the fact that he risks
drawing it when it isn't useful and now is his payoff. And especially
the fact that you're not just randomly forcing him to discard any
card makes the action a significant punishment. You're forcing him
to discard a card that you know about *only* because it was useful at
that moment. He may have been holding onto that card for six turns
waiting for the situation to come up so he could play the card.

From the perspective of other players who don't know what a non-
revealed card is, it may seem neutral to force a player to discard
and draw another unseen card. But from the perspective of the player
who built the deck and is constantly dealing with his draws and
arranging to make plays and do discards so that he can have in his
hand what he wants to have at any given moment, forcing a discard is
a positive punishment. And as such, it should be reserved for
situations when that player seems to have revealed the card as a
deliberate act to gain significant advantage.

>> Now, if the player intentionally showed the card, that's a different
>> story.
>
> Absolutely. I am talking about the more comlicated case of accidentally
> showing.

And therefore, it is unclear why the player deserves to be punished for
it.

Fred

I agree with Fred regarding the severity of forcing a player to
reshuffle a significant card (DT.)

If I were judging and someone accidentally revealed the DT (which seems
unlikely), I would perhaps do the following:

Take the player aside, and let them know I'm going to tell the table
that he can't play that DT this vote. But, I will actually allow him
to play it if he wants. Then go back to the table and tell them he
can't play the DT, but if he has a second one in his hand, he can play
that one. After the vote is resolved, tell the table the truth.

Thoughts for a better solution?

Ira

Perhaps the thing to do in this case is ask the player who revealed the
card for that card and the bottom card of his library (unrevealed). Mix
the two up, and have the player select one of them to return to his
hand. The other card goes back to the bottom of the library. Perhaps
the game state is changed, perhaps not. Only the 'punished' player
knows for sure. In our hypothetical, the acting player KNOWS there's a
50/50 chance the card could be played, which is still more info than he
had before the reveal.

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <F9Bff.551$1x.297@fed1read06>, Fred Scott

<nos...@no.spam.dot.com> writes:
>I'm sorry, I'm not seeing how there being only 50% chance of the wrong
>thing happening makes it all right. You shouldn't be messing with the
>guy's hand. That's wrong.

In this specific instance, it may be.

However, more generally, a judge has to do what he sees as being right
at the time to restore the Game State. 200 in the judging guidelines
covers a few examples.

In the examples, there are some quite wide-ranging corrections shown.
The point is that the judge will usually have to think of something on
the hoof, and this may not be easy. (Of course, in the instance of
common infractions, it might be possible to extend the examples to give
more guidance.)

In the instance of someone calling a significant political action and
being threatened with DT (or Vox Domini etc.), the game state is such
that all the cards are where they are (obviously) but also that the
acting Methuselah is unsure of whether a person really has a DT. Are
they bluffing? Should I negotiate with them before I set the terms? Do
they have a history of vote cancellation tactics?

Restoring the obvious game state in this instance is trivial (move
things the DT-threatening player accidentally dropped back to his hand),
but a conscientious judge may also wish to attempt to restore the
uncertainty. This assumes that the acting Methuselah hadn't seen the DT
earlier - say, with a Revelations etc. - which hadn't later been
discarded.

Even if accidentally done, if the acting Methuselah *knows* I have a DT,
I have a potential negotiating edge over when I just threaten that I
have one. Even unintentional fractions shouldn't - where possible -
lead to an advantage of that sort.

Of course, when looking at the examples of state correction, there is no
attempt to allow the restored vampire (for example) to do anything other
than hunt over the two turns it was burned, because this would be
significant and difficult to simulate. (One might also view this as a
good reason for players to be more familiar with the rules, so that they
don't find themselves on the sharp end of this.) However, when the
infraction has happened *right now*, it may be possible to intervene
more ably.

Is fiddling with their hand going to cause more trouble than it's worth?
Possibly, possibly not.

An alternative to hand fiddling might be to take the player to one side,
toss a coin (or roll a die etc.) and, depending on the outcome, let them
play it or not. They can *threaten* all they want, regardless of the
outcome of the random factor, but their hand is left exactly as it was
before the accident.

--
James Coupe

Sure. I agree. With a card revealed, the game state is unquestionably
different.

> Restoring the obvious game state in this instance is trivial (move
> things the DT-threatening player accidentally dropped back to his hand),
> but a conscientious judge may also wish to attempt to restore the
> uncertainty.

Right. What Ira proposed was complex but it was pretty clear in its
intent.

> Is fiddling with their hand going to cause more trouble than it's worth?
> Possibly, possibly not.

I guess what I'm saying is that in most cases, it shouldn't be done. It
isn't a question of how much trouble it's worth, not being sure what
you mean by "trouble". (They never pay a judge enough for his troubles,
anyway.) I mean that altering the player's hand is almost always far more
unfair than just letting the lack of the usual uncertainty stand. I would
make exceptions, of course, when the player who revealed the card seemed
to have done so deliberately (understanding that it's sometimes a trick to
read his mind). Then I wouldn't be so opposed to replacing the card.

I think that people are getting so caught up in how to solve the problem of
reinserting uncertainty into the situation that they're forgetting that
most of the solutions are worse than the original problem.

Fred

he's done something the judge disapproves of but is not actually
illegal. (And I get the distinct impression that this is the only
reason Frank suggested it be considered stalling.) A player will
typically stall when he feels his position will be better off if
it the games ends with less development than it could reach under
normal circumstances. The usual scenario is that the player
attempting to stall is himself at risk of being ousted but might
survive to the time limit if the game proceeds more slowly. This
is not the only possible reason, however.

Alternatively, stalling is sometimes ruled for other reasons such
as players habitually engaging in activity which has no point to
it in terms of the game, like endlessly negotiating deals that
don't seem likely to get made and/or accomplish little if they
are made. In this case, the point of the ruling is to get the
players to play in a manner in line with the intent of the game
rather than regulate unfair behavior. This is also not indicated
by the scenario suggested unless the player was habitually reading
unimportant card text from *every* card that he drew. But that
wasn't what you were talking about when you originally proposed
it.

> Would this fall under of the category of something not specifically
> against any rule but commonly agreed as something one should not do?

No. It's totally fine.

Fred
